sections.title: The conditional: the "would" form
sections.content: You know *szeretnék* as one ready-made phrase. It is the verb *szeretni* in the conditional, the “would” form. The conditional puts *-n-* and a vowel between the stem and the person ending: for *én* it is *-nék*, for *te* *-nél*, for *ő* *-ne*. So *szeret* + *-nék* = *szeretnék* (I would like). *Kér* works the same way, and *kérnék* is a softer *kérek*.

sections.title: Asking politely
sections.content: *Kérek* is clear and normal in a café. *Kérnék* and *szeretnék* are softer. A waiter who does not know you uses the *ő* form for “you”: *Mit szeretne?* (What would you like?) Between friends, say *Mit szeretnél?*

items.english: What would you like? (to a stranger)

sections.content: Do not mix up *kérnék* (I would like) with *kérnek* (they ask for): the *é* makes the difference. Verbs with back vowels use *-nál* and *-na* instead of *-nél* and *-ne* (*olvasnál*, *olvasna*), but *én* is always *-nék* (*olvasnék*); the two verbs here have front vowels.
